title: Two Indian Crew Members Safe After MV Hondius Hantavirus Scare
excerpt: India's Madrid embassy confirms both nationals are asymptomatic and now in quarantine in the Netherlands after evacuating the outbreak-hit ship.
body:
Two Indian nationals serving as crew aboard the Dutch expedition vessel MV Hondius arrived safely in the Netherlands on Sunday after Spanish authorities evacuated them from the hantavirus-stricken ship as it anchored off Spain's Canary Islands.

**What happened:**
Both Indian crew members were evacuated to the Netherlands for quarantine after the ship arrived off the Canary Islands on Sunday. The Embassy of India in Madrid confirmed that the two Indians were 'healthy and asymptomatic' as Spanish authorities enforced strict international health protocols. Indian Ambassador to Spain Jayant N. Khobragade is in close contact with Spanish authorities and the two Indian nationals to assure their safety and well-being.

**Why this outbreak alarmed the world:**
The luxury cruise ship, operated by Oceanwide Expeditions, began its journey on April 1 from Argentina's Ushuaia and arrived in Spain's Canary Islands on Sunday after the virus outbreak was reported. As of May 8, a total of eight cases including three deaths — a case fatality ratio of 38% — have been reported, with six cases laboratory-confirmed as Andes virus. The Andes virus — identified in this outbreak — is one of the only hantavirus strains confirmed to transmit between humans under certain conditions, a fact that drove heightened concern among international health agencies. WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus confirmed that WHO experts on the ground are working with Spain's Health Ministry on epidemiological assessment and coordinating charter flights for passengers.

**What to watch next:**
Health officials in at least a dozen countries are monitoring passengers who dispersed around the world after the hantavirus outbreak killed three people. WHO advises that all passengers and crew practice active symptom monitoring for 45 days after exposure.
